n: The book opens with a funeral cry: “How…!” Jerusalem, once crowded and honored among nations, now sits empty like a widow and pays tribute to a foreign master. Chapters 1–4 are acrostic poems, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

f.g: Hebrew ’ekah, the book’s Hebrew title; a typical opening for a funeral dirge (compare Isaiah 1:21).
Forced to pay tribute; reduced to a servant state.

n: Jerusalem is pictured as a woman weeping alone at night. The “lovers” and “friends” are the foreign allies (like Egypt) Judah trusted instead of the Lord; they gave no help when Babylon came.

f.g: Political allies and foreign gods that Judah courted.

n: Judah has gone into exile after suffering and hard bondage. Living among foreign nations, she finds no rest; her enemies caught her in a narrow place with no escape.

f.g: In tight places—trapped like prey in a narrow pass.

n: Even the roads to Jerusalem seem to mourn because no pilgrims travel them for the holy festivals. The temple’s worship has stopped, and priests and young women alike grieve.

f.g: The appointed festivals such as Passover and Tabernacles, when Israel gathered at the temple.

n: Her enemies are now on top. The poet is honest about why: the Lord allowed this because of Judah’s many sins, just as the covenant had warned.

f.w: her children are gone into captivity

n: Zion’s glory is gone. Her leaders are like starving deer that can no longer run, fleeing helplessly—perhaps recalling King Zedekiah’s failed escape from the city.

f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem and its people, personified as a young woman.

f.w: they are gone without strength before the pursuer

n: In her misery Jerusalem remembers better days. When she fell, no one helped, and her enemies laughed at her ruin, even mocking the sabbaths that marked her as the Lord’s people.

f.g: Some translations read “downfall” or “ceasing”; either way her collapse became a joke to her foes.

n: The poet does not excuse Jerusalem: she sinned seriously, and so she was removed. Those who once admired her now despise her, seeing her shame exposed.

f.g: A picture of public disgrace and exposure.

n: Her uncleanness clings to her clothing; she never considered where her choices would lead. Her fall was astonishing. Suddenly Jerusalem herself cries out to the Lord to see her pain.

f.w: she remembereth not her last end
f.g: She did not think about the consequences of her actions.
Astonishingly, in a shocking way.

n: The enemy has grabbed all her treasures—worst of all, foreigners walked into the temple itself, a holy place the law said they must not enter.

f.w: the heathen entered into her sanctuary

n: Famine is so severe that people trade their treasures just for food to stay alive. Jerusalem again turns directly to the Lord: “See how worthless I have become.”

f.g: Food of any kind (KJV English).
To keep themselves alive.

n: One of the most famous lines in Lamentations: Jerusalem calls to passersby, “Is there any sorrow like my sorrow?” Christians have long heard in it an echo of the suffering Savior, whose pain went beyond all others.

f.w: Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?
the day of his fierce anger

n: Jerusalem describes judgment as fire in her bones, a hunting net around her feet, and a long sickness that leaves her faint all day long.

f.w: he hath spread a net for my feet

n: Her sins have become like a heavy yoke the Lord fastens on her neck—sin itself becomes the burden that drags her down into captivity.

f.g: A wooden collar for oxen; a symbol of servitude.

n: The Lord has crushed her soldiers and young men as grapes are trampled in a winepress. The winepress image of judgment reappears in later scripture concerning the Lord’s coming.

f.w: the virgin, the daughter of Judah
f.g: Poetic title for the people of Judah as a once-protected daughter.

n: Jerusalem weeps endlessly. The repetition “mine eye, mine eye” shows overwhelming grief. The comforter who should revive her is far away, and her children are ruined.

f.g: One who would bring relief or restore life; the word recurs through this chapter (vv. 2, 9, 17, 21).

n: The narrator returns: Zion stretches out her hands for help, but no one comes. The Lord has let Jacob’s neighbors become his enemies, and they treat Jerusalem as ritually unclean.

f.g: A gesture of pleading or prayer.
Under the law of Moses, someone ritually unclean and kept apart; here a picture of being shunned.

n: A turning point of honesty: “The Lord is righteous; I rebelled.” Jerusalem accepts responsibility, the first step of real repentance, and asks the nations to see her suffering.
She called for her allies, but they betrayed her. Even priests and elders died of hunger while searching for food in the besieged city.

f.g: Died.
Searched for food.

n: Jerusalem cries out in anguish, confessing her rebellion. Outside the city the sword kills; inside, famine and disease bring death—there is no safe place.

f.g: Hebrew idiom: my inner being is in turmoil (the bowels were seen as the seat of emotions).

f.w: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death

n: Her enemies rejoice that God has punished her. Yet she trusts that the day of judgment the Lord has announced will come on them too.

f.w: the day that thou hast called
f.g: The day of the Lord’s judgment proclaimed by the prophets.

n: The poem closes with a plea for justice: let the wickedness of Judah’s enemies come before God as hers has. Her sighs are many and her heart is faint—grief without easy answers.

f.w: Let all their wickedness come before thee
